lead: The Myhill-Nerode theorem turns a question about machines into a question about strings. Two strings are equivalent for a language L when no suffix can tell them apart: for every z, xz and yz are both in L or both outside L. If L has finitely many such classes, L is regular, and the class count is exactly the state count of its smallest DFA. If there are infinitely many classes, L is not regular. The theorem is used to prove non-regularity cleanly and to justify DFA minimization. Some syllabi spell it Myhill–Nerode.
prereq: You need: DFA and extended transition function from Unit 1, and the pumping lemma from Chapter 2.6.

blocks.text: Fix an alphabet Σ and a language L ⊆ Σ*. For strings x, y ∈ Σ*, write x ≡_L y when for every suffix z ∈ Σ*, xz ∈ L exactly when yz ∈ L. The suffix may be empty, so equivalent strings agree on membership themselves. This relation is an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, and transitive by using the same z. It is also a right congruence: if x ≡_L y, then xa ≡_L ya for every symbol a ∈ Σ: for every suffix z, xaz ∈ L exactly when yaz ∈ L; since az is just some suffix of x and y, xa ≡_L ya. The index of ≡_L is its number of classes.

The link to machines is direct. In a DFA for L, after reading x the machine is in state δ*(q0, x). The future depends only on this state: the set of suffixes accepted from it. If x and y reach the same state, they are ≡_L. A DFA with n states therefore gives at most n classes. Two different states may still be equivalent if the DFA is not minimal. Classes are sets of strings, not states themselves.

sections.h3: The theorem and the minimal DFA

blocks.text: L is regular ⇔ ≡_L has finitely many classes
blocks.where: L is a language over Σ; ≡_L compares strings by every suffix z; the number of classes is the index.

blocks.text: If ≡_L has finitely many classes, build a DFA whose states are the classes [x]. The start state is [ε]. On symbol a, go from [x] to [xa]. Make [x] accepting when x ∈ L. Right congruence makes the transition well defined: if x ≡_L y, then xa ≡_L ya. This DFA accepts exactly L. So finite index implies regular.

If L is regular with a DFA M of n states, map each string x to the state reached after x. This gives at most n classes, so the index is finite. Thus regular implies finite index. The constructed DFA is minimal. If x and y are distinguishable, some z puts xz in L and yz outside L. No DFA can end in the same state after x and y, because then it would treat suffix z identically. So each class needs its own state. The number of classes equals the states of the minimal DFA. This matches DFA minimization in Unit 1: equivalent states correspond to classes of their access strings.

To prove L is not regular, exhibit an infinite set S ⊆ Σ* whose strings are pairwise distinguishable. For every two different x, y ∈ S there is a suffix z, depending on x and y, with exactly one of xz, yz in L. Then x and y lie in different ≡_L classes. Infinite S means infinitely many classes. By the theorem, L is not regular. The suffix need not be the same for every pair; it only must separate that pair.

The standard pattern uses L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ | n ≥ 0}. The strings 0ⁱ are pairwise distinguishable. For i ≠ j, choose suffix 1ⁱ. Then 0ⁱ1ⁱ ∈ L, but 0ʲ1ⁱ ∉ L because the counts of zeros and ones differ. Hence infinitely many classes exist and L is not regular. The figure shows the 4×4 table for i, j = 0,1,2,3; the diagonal marks membership.
Do not confuse an infinite language with infinite index. Σ* is infinite and regular: every string is equivalent because every concatenation stays in Σ*. The index counts classes, not strings.

examples.question: Let L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ | n ≥ 0}. Use the Myhill-Nerode theorem to prove L is not regular. Take the four strings 0⁰, 0¹, 0², 0³. Show they are pairwise distinguishable by suffix 1ⁱ, and state how many distinct equivalence classes these four strings represent.
steps: Write x_i = 0ⁱ for i = 0,1,2,3. These are the four strings ε, 0, 00, 000.
For a pair i ≠ j, choose suffix z = 1ⁱ. Then x_i z = 0ⁱ1ⁱ has i zeros and i ones, so it is in L.
For the same suffix, x_j z = 0ʲ1ⁱ has j zeros and i ones. Since j ≠ i, it is not in L.
So every pair x_i, x_j with i ≠ j is distinguished by some suffix. The suffix may depend on the pair; here it is 1ⁱ.
Therefore the four strings lie in four different classes of ≡_L. Count = 4.
Extend the same argument to all k ≥ 0: 0ᵏ is distinguished from every 0ʲ with j ≠ k by suffix 1ᵏ. The set {0ᵏ | k ≥ 0} is infinite and pairwise distinguishable.
By the Myhill-Nerode theorem, L has infinitely many classes, so L is not regular.
examples.answer: The four strings represent 4 distinct classes; since the family 0ⁱ (i ≥ 0) is infinite and pairwise distinguishable, L is not regular.

traps: You need infinitely many pairwise distinguishable strings, not just an infinite language. Σ* is infinite and regular with one class.
A suffix may depend on the pair of strings being separated. Do not demand one suffix work for every pair at once.
The index equals the number of states of the minimal DFA, not the number of states of any DFA you happen to draw.

Two strings can both be in L (or both outside L) and still not be equivalent, because a longer suffix may separate them. For example in L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ}, the strings 0 and 00 are both outside L, yet suffix 1 puts 01 in L and 001 outside.

quiz.a: A language L is regular if and only if ≡_L has finitely many equivalence classes. When L is regular, this number equals the number of states in the minimal DFA for L.

quiz.q: Why does a DFA with n states give at most n classes of ≡_L?
quiz.a: Each string x leads to one state after reading x. Strings that reach the same state accept exactly the same suffixes, so they are equivalent. There are at most n states, hence at most n classes.

quiz.q: For L = {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0}, which suffix distinguishes aⁱ and aʲ when i ≠ j?
quiz.a: Use suffix bⁱ. Then aⁱbⁱ ∈ L, but aʲbⁱ ∉ L because the numbers of a's and b's differ. So aⁱ and aʲ are distinguishable.

quiz.q: A language has exactly 5 Myhill-Nerode classes. What can you say about its minimal DFA?
quiz.a: The minimal DFA has exactly 5 states. Each class becomes one state, and distinguishable classes cannot be merged.

quiz.q: Let L = {w ∈ {0,1}* | w has equal numbers of 0s and 1s}. Using strings 0ⁱ for i ≥ 0, prove L is not regular.
quiz.a: For i ≠ j, choose suffix 1ⁱ. The string 0ⁱ1ⁱ is balanced and in L. The string 0ʲ1ⁱ is unbalanced and not in L. Thus the infinitely many strings 0ⁱ are pairwise distinguishable, so L is not regular.

quiz.q: True or false: every infinite language has infinitely many Myhill-Nerode classes. Explain.
quiz.a: False. Σ* is infinite and regular. Every string is equivalent because every concatenation remains in Σ*, so there is only one class.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Myhill-Nerode congruence is the idea behind DFA minimization in compiler lexers and regular-expression engines. In automata learning, the Nerode congruence helps build a DFA from membership queries and counterexamples. In verification, it supports equivalence checks between regular specifications. Search for Myhill-Nerode congruence, DFA minimization, and automata learning.
